Spring Equinox. Also called the vernal equinox, it marks the astronomical moment when the sun crosses the celestial equator, making day and night nearly equal length across the globe. Occurring around March twentieth in the Northern Hemisphere, this transitional point has anchored human calendars, mythologies, and renewal celebrations for millennia, signaling the return of growth and fertility after winter dormancy.

The spring equinox occurs when the sun is directly above the equator, creating a moment when the plane of Earth's equator and the plane of its orbit around the sun align. The exact date varies slightly year to year based on Earth's orbital mechanics, but centers around March twentieth to twenty-first in the Northern Hemisphere.

It is called the vernal equinox because "vernal" derives from the Latin vernus for spring, distinguishing it from the autumnal equinox in September, which is essentially its opposite in Earth's orbit.

In the Northern Hemisphere, it marks the astronomical beginning of spring. In the Southern Hemisphere, it coincides with the autumn equinox, approximately September twenty-second to twenty-third, creating a mirror-image seasonal rhythm.

The name equinox derives from Latin meaning "equal night," because day and night are nearly equal in length—approximately twelve hours each—at this moment worldwide.

The spring equinox was pivotal for ancient agricultural societies, whose planting calendars and crop prayers were synchronized to this moment of solar alignment. Farming communities depended on precise knowledge of this astronomical event.

It is encoded into countless cultural and religious observances—Nowruz in the Persian tradition, Songkran in Southeast Asia, and many pre-Christian fertility rites across Europe, the Mediterranean, and Asia.

The spring equinox creates a moment of cosmic symmetry that has resonated symbolically across human cultures as a gateway between seasons, metaphorically representing rebirth and renewal, much like the autumn equinox marks transition into dormancy.
